title: 2 Samuel 18:19–33
context: Ahimaaz and a Cushite run to bring David the news. David waits between the gates, asking each runner whether it is well with the young man Absalom. When the Cushite’s answer makes the truth plain, David goes up to the room over the gate and weeps for his son. Versification: English 18:33 is Hebrew 19:1; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, “Let me now run and carry the king news, how the LORD has avenged him of his enemies.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimaaz asks to run with news of how the LORD has avenged the king. Arminian readers note his eagerness to share what he sees as good news, without fully grasping how David will receive it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Ahimaaz frames the victory as God’s vindication of David, which is true. Yet he misses that for David the news carries deep personal grief.

verses.text: Joab said to him, “You must not be the bearer of news today, but you must carry news another day. But today you must carry no news, because the king’s son is dead.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joab tells Ahimaaz not to carry news today because the king’s son is dead. Arminian readers see Joab protecting Ahimaaz from delivering painful news, perhaps aware of how David treated earlier messengers (1:15; 4:10-12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joab recognizes what the victory will mean to David. The death of Absalom makes this day both triumph and tragedy. Joab’s words show he knows it.

verses.text: Then Joab said to the Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen!” The Cushite bowed himself to Joab, and ran.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab sends the Cushite to tell the king what he saw. Arminian readers note that the Cushite obeys promptly and runs, a faithful servant fulfilling an unwelcome duty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Joab chooses a foreigner for the task, perhaps one less exposed to the king’s displeasure. The narrator does not explain his reasons.

verses.text: Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said yet again to Joab, “But come what may, please let me also run after the Cushite.” Joab said, “Why do you want to run, my son, since you will have no reward for the news?”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimaaz asks again to run, come what may, and Joab asks why when there is no reward. Arminian readers see persistent zeal, though perhaps mixed with a desire to be the bearer of news.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Joab’s fatherly address, my son, and his warning that the news brings no reward. Ahimaaz’s insistence shows how strongly he wishes to serve the king.

verses.text: “But come what may,” he said, “I will run.” He said to him, “Run!” Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the Plain, and outran the Cushite.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimaaz runs by the way of the Plain and outruns the Cushite. Arminian readers note his determination and the choice of a faster route. Speed, however, is not the same as candor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that being first does not mean bringing the full truth. Ahimaaz will arrive first but avoid telling the king what he most needs to know.

verses.text: Now David was sitting between the two gates; and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate to the wall, and lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, a man running alone.
verses.arminianNotes: David sits between the two gates while the watchman looks out and sees a man running alone. Arminian readers feel the tension of a father waiting for news of his son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of the king at the gate, where he had stood as the army went out (18:4). The narrator slows the scene to heighten the suspense.

verses.text: The watchman shouted and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, there is news in his mouth.” He came closer and closer.
verses.arminianNotes: David says that a lone runner brings news. Arminian readers note his hopeful reasoning, reading the runner as a sign of victory rather than rout.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David interprets signs with hope. A fleeing army would come in groups, so a single runner suggests a messenger. Hope shapes how he reads the scene.

verses.text: The watchman saw another man running; and the watchman called to the gatekeeper and said, “Behold, a man running alone!” The king said, “He also brings news.”
verses.arminianNotes: The watchman sees a second man running alone, and David concludes that he too brings news. Arminian readers note the father’s growing anticipation, clinging to hope as each messenger approaches.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator building slowly toward the moment of truth. The repeated sightings keep the king, and the reader, fixed on one question: what has happened to Absalom.

verses.text: The watchman said, “I think the running of the first one is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok.” The king said, “He is a good man, and comes with good news.”
verses.arminianNotes: The watchman recognizes Ahimaaz by the way he runs, and David calls him a good man who brings good news. Arminian readers note David’s trust in a messenger whose loyalty he knows well.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe David’s hopeful assumption that a good man must carry good news. The assumption will be painfully tested, since good men can also bring the hardest tidings.

verses.text: Ahimaaz called, and said to the king, “All is well.” He bowed himself before the king with his face to the earth, and said, “Blessed is the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who lifted up their hand against my lord the king!”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimaaz announces all is well and blesses the LORD for delivering the king’s enemies. Arminian readers see sincere praise for God’s deliverance of David. He leads with what will please the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ahimaaz rightly credits the LORD with the victory. His words echo the theme that God, not human strength, decides the outcome.

verses.text: The king said, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?” Ahimaaz answered, “When Joab sent the king’s servant, even me your servant, I saw a great tumult, but I don’t know what it was.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks about Absalom, and Ahimaaz says he saw a tumult but does not know what it was. Arminian readers note his evasion, perhaps out of fear or compassion, avoiding the painful truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Ahimaaz knew Absalom was dead (18:20) but does not say so. His evasion delays the king’s grief but cannot prevent it.

verses.text: The king said, “Come and stand here.” He came and stood still.
verses.arminianNotes: David tells Ahimaaz to stand aside, and he stands still. Arminian readers note the quiet tension of this moment, when Ahimaaz’s evasion has bought only a brief delay before the truth arrives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pause as a deliberate narrative beat. The king sets aside the messenger who would not answer and waits for the one who will, keeping the focus on Absalom.

verses.text: Behold, the Cushite came. The Cushite said, “Good news for my lord the king, for the LORD has avenged you today of all those who rose up against you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Cushite arrives announcing good news, that the LORD has vindicated David against all who rose up. Arminian readers note that he, like the first runner, speaks of the victory as an act of divine justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that both messengers attribute the victory to the LORD. The theology is sound, but the king’s heart is focused on one person.

verses.text: The king said to the Cushite, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?” The Cushite answered, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you to do you harm, be as that young man is.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks the Cushite whether it is well with Absalom, and he replies that the king’s enemies should be as that young man. Arminian readers see a tactful but unmistakable report of Absalom’s death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the Cushite tells the truth without stating it bluntly, blending loyalty to the king with honesty about the outcome. David understands at once what has happened.

verses.text: The king was much moved, and went up to the room over the gate and wept. As he went, he said, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! I wish I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son!”
verses.arminianNotes: David weeps and cries, My son Absalom! I wish I had died instead of you. Arminian readers see the depth of a father’s grief, and they note how sin’s consequences, foretold in 12:10, wound even those who are forgiven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in David’s wish to die in Absalom’s place a longing that only Christ fulfills, the one who died for rebels (Romans 5:8). They also urge that David’s grief be met with pastoral tenderness rather than turned quickly into a lesson.
